newsitem.title: FRANCE: France's GAN expects bank arm sold first.
newsitem.headline: France's GAN expects bank arm sold first.

text.p: French government-controlled insurer GAN said on Tuesday its CIC banking arm was likely to be privatised ahead of its insurance activities and both should be sold before the end of the year.
Chairman Didier Pfeiffer said he had hoped to privatise the two together "but when we look at the national and international players, it seemed very difficult to achieve".

"This has led us to look at doing the two privatisations separately and the feeling is that it is better to privatise CIC before GAN," he said, adding that it was the best way to maintain the bancassurance links between the two companies.
GAN is hoping that after CIC is sold it will remain the second largest shareholder in the bank with a stake "that would not be below 20 percent". It currently has 93 percent.

Pfeiffer, appointed last November after the government fired his predecessor, was speaking at a news conference to discuss the 80.5 percent state-owned company's higher-than-expected 1996 loss of 5.68 billion francs ($974 million), reported late on Monday.
The losses -- estimated at five billion francs by the government in February -- included provisions of 13.8 billion for bad real estate loans and investments accumulated by several of GAN's units.
The 1996 loss compared with a 1995 deficit of 1.79 billion francs.
GAN has been promised a government aid package of at least 20 billion francs to ready it for sale.
The state's first attempt to sell CIC last year was abandoned in the face of widespread opposition. Bids from French banks BNP and Societe Generale were received but judged unsatisfactory.
CIC made a 1996 net profit of 847 million francs, up 36 percent from a year earlier.

The state has agreed to inject 11 billion into parent group GAN this year, including 7.1 billion to recapitalise what Finance Minister Jean Arthuis called its"diseased" UIC property banking subsidiary and a further 3.9 billion to bring the resources of its insurance activities up to acceptable regulatory levels.
The government has promised to cover losses on bad loans to property developers and losses on property sales and estimated the cost of that operation at a further nine billion francs.
Pfeiffer said after a thorough cleanup of 1996 accounts, CIC and GAN would be "free of the need for exceptional charges which weighed on them in the past".
The time now appeared ripe for GAN's privatisation which "could come as of this financial exercise", he said.
GAN's recapitalisation is expected to be carried out this summer. The method should be settled at a board meeting prior to the June 25 annual shareholders' meeting.

Pfeiffer said that the state aid was an integral part of GAN's 1996 accounts and it was essential that the European Union, which must clear state help, decided whether to approve the aid before the shareholders' meeting.
Pfeiffer said GAN's purchaser would need to be involved in complementary activities.
He indicated that his group was proceeding in a systematic fashion to examine GAN's similiarities with potential partners, which he said included AGF, Allianz, Fortis, Generali and ING.
As far as CIC is concerned, other French or foreign banks could be interested apart from BNP and Societe Generale, which had shown their interest during the initial but now defunct sale tender.
CIC is valued in GAN's book at a total 14.6 billion francs while the previous offers were around 10 billion francs.
